diagnostic_cards.title: RS485 DE timing wrong with UART
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: RS485 communication is unstable with missing first bytes, truncated tail bytes, or random frame corruption.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Half-duplex RS485 using USART hardware DE or GPIO-based DE control, often after baud or frame format changes.
likely_causes: DE polarity is inverted versus transceiver enable expectation
DE assertion starts too late relative to first UART start bit
DE deassertion happens before end of last stop bit
DEAT and DEDT values are too short for selected baud rate
RE and DE pin mapping on transceiver is mismatched
confirmed_facts: RS485 direction control timing must bracket full UART frame transmission
Wrong DE polarity or timing can cause clipped or colliding frames
Oscilloscope capture of TX and DE is the fastest way to confirm timing faults
plausible_diagnosis: Late DE assertion causes first-byte loss
Early DE release truncates CRC or final payload bytes
Intermittent bus contention indicates two active transmitters
debug_checks: Confirm USART mode and half-duplex configuration consistency
Measure DE high window against TX waveform on scope
Sweep DEAT and DEDT margins while keeping payload constant
Verify transceiver RE and DE pins and polarity in board schematic
Check UART frame settings parity stop bits and word length on both nodes
possible_workarounds: Temporarily control DE by GPIO around transmit calls to validate root cause
Increase DEAT and DEDT values with conservative timing margins
Lower baud rate to reduce boundary sensitivity during triage
constraints_or_limits: Requires board-level transceiver wiring information
Scope-based validation is required for high confidence closure
No claim of upstream firmware fix status without explicit issue or PR evidence

diagnostic_cards.title: USB HS with ULPI does not start
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: USB HS host or device does not enumerate and appears dead at startup with external ULPI PHY.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Custom boards or bring-up phases using USB_OTG_HS with external PHY and cache DMA interactions.
likely_causes: ULPI reference clock is absent unstable or not routed
PHY reset and power sequencing is incorrect
ULPI pin alternate function mapping is incomplete
Host and device init order conflicts with clock setup
DMA cache region is configured with incompatible MPU attributes
confirmed_facts: ULPI HS operation depends on external PHY clock and reset readiness
USB DMA and cache configuration can produce startup anomalies on H7
Wrong low-level init order can block USB state machine progression
plausible_diagnosis: No clock at PHY implies immediate bring-up failure
Enumeration stalls after a few transfers indicate cache DMA coherency gap
Intermittent startup behavior often points to reset timing race
debug_checks: Measure ULPI clock at PHY and MCU pins
Validate PHY reset pulse width and post-reset delay
Audit pinmux and alternate functions for ULPI data and control lines
Check USB RAM placement and MPU cacheability attributes
Run minimal host-only and device-only test paths separately
possible_workarounds: Temporarily run with reduced complexity host-only path
Use non-cacheable DMA buffers in validated SRAM region
Add conservative delays after PHY reset and clock stabilization
constraints_or_limits: Board-specific PHY design is a major variable
Cannot claim universal fix without exact PHY part and schematic
Evidence is pattern-based and requires lab validation

diagnostic_cards.title: USB CDC plus RTOS random blocking writes
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: CDC writes block unpredictably under RTOS load with occasional hangs or throughput collapse.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Multiple tasks writing to CDC transport while ISR callbacks and USB stack state transitions are active.
likely_causes: Concurrent writers access CDC TX path without single ownership
Blocking write API is called from timing-sensitive task context
Queue and ISR handoff is missing backpressure policy
TX complete callback and task signaling have race conditions
Cache DMA side effects amplify timing jitter
confirmed_facts: CDC TX paths are sensitive to concurrent access patterns
Single-producer ownership significantly reduces deadlock risk
Non-blocking queue-based architecture is generally safer in RTOS
plausible_diagnosis: Random stalls map to lock inversion between task and callback
Hangs under high traffic indicate missing backpressure or retry strategy
Mixed blocking and ISR-driven flows create non-deterministic latency
debug_checks: Enforce one task as exclusive CDC TX owner
Instrument queue depth and TX completion latency
Audit mutex semaphore usage between ISR and task contexts
Reject blocking CDC writes from high-priority control tasks
Trace timeout and retry counters under load
possible_workarounds: Introduce queue-based TX worker task with bounded buffer
Switch to non-blocking send with explicit retry policy
Throttle producer tasks when queue watermark is exceeded
constraints_or_limits: Final fix depends on application task model
No guaranteed upstream fix for all CDC RTOS concurrency patterns
Requires runtime tracing to confirm race conditions

diagnostic_cards.title: ADC wrong readings with high-impedance source
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: ADC values drift clip or depend on channel order when source impedance is high.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Sensors with high source resistance multiplexed channel scans or short sampling windows.
likely_causes: Sample and hold capacitor does not settle within configured sampling time
Input source impedance exceeds practical range for chosen sample cycles
Back-to-back channel scanning causes charge sharing artifacts
No analog buffer op-amp between sensor and ADC input
ADC clock or prescaler is too aggressive for front-end dynamics
confirmed_facts: High source impedance increases settling-time requirements
Sampling-time configuration directly impacts conversion accuracy
Channel sequence can affect measured value in multiplexed scans
plausible_diagnosis: Order-dependent errors indicate incomplete S and H settling
Values improve at lower ADC clock or longer sample times
Buffering the source removes most drift and crosstalk
debug_checks: Increase sampling time and compare conversion stability
Measure source impedance and compute settling margin
Insert dummy conversion after channel switch
Reorder channels to isolate crosstalk-sensitive inputs
Validate analog reference and ground integrity
possible_workarounds: Use longer sample time and lower ADC clock
Add op-amp buffer for high-impedance sensors
Separate critical channels into independent conversion groups
constraints_or_limits: Exact settling budget depends on sensor and board analog design
Firmware-only mitigation may be insufficient for very high impedance
Needs hardware measurement to confirm final root cause

diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Bring-up on NUCLEO or custom boards with mixed classical CAN and FDCAN settings.
likely_causes: No external CAN transceiver or transceiver enable pin not asserted
Global filter rejects all non-matching frames
Message RAM layout overlaps or wrong offset configuration
Nominal bit timing does not match bus parameters
RX FIFO interrupt is not enabled or routed
confirmed_facts: Many NUCLEO setups require external transceiver for real bus communication
Global filter defaults can silently drop frames
Message RAM misconfiguration can make RX path appear dead
plausible_diagnosis: No bus traffic at transceiver pins indicates hardware-layer gap
Traffic visible on bus but none in FIFO suggests filter or RAM config issue
Intermittent receive only at low speed indicates timing mismatch
debug_checks: Verify transceiver presence power and standby pins
Set permissive global filter and explicit standard ID filter for test
Validate message RAM offsets against reference and HAL config
Cross-check nominal data timing with known-good node
Confirm RX FIFO interrupt enable and NVIC mapping
possible_workarounds: Start with loopback mode then move to normal mode
Use broad filter during bring-up before narrowing IDs
Use known-good evaluation board timing profile as baseline
constraints_or_limits: Requires physical bus and transceiver verification
Cannot infer bus integrity from firmware logs alone
Board-specific wiring errors can mimic software faults

Controller not re-enabled after bus-off handling
Error interrupts are not serviced or recovery path is absent
Transceiver remains in standby or silent mode

Physical bus integrity must be validated before software recovery
Recovery often requires explicit controller sequence depending on stack design
plausible_diagnosis: Immediate re-entry to bus-off indicates unresolved physical-layer fault
No recovery with healthy bus indicates controller re-enable path is missing
Recovery only at reduced bitrate suggests timing margin issue

Verify nominal and data phase timing with known-good node
Inspect bus-off interrupt handling and re-enable sequence
Check transceiver mode pins standby enable and silent settings
Log TEC and REC progression before and after bus-off

Perform full controller stop and re-init after bus-off

constraints_or_limits: Cannot confirm root cause without physical bus measurements

diagnostic_cards.title: SDMMC plus FatFS corrupted files with DMA

diagnostic_cards.affected_context: H7 projects using SDMMC and FatFS with DMA and data cache enabled under RTOS or heavy I O.
likely_causes: DCache clean invalidate policy not aligned with DMA direction
Sector buffers are not properly aligned for DMA access
Buffers are allocated in cacheable region without coherency management
FatFS buffer ownership overlaps with asynchronous DMA transactions
SDMMC and MDMA integration order is misconfigured
confirmed_facts: Cache DMA coherency is a common root cause of storage corruption on H7
Buffer alignment and memory placement directly affect SDMMC DMA reliability
RTOS timing can expose hidden ownership races in file I O path
plausible_diagnosis: Corruption after stress writes indicates missing cache maintenance
Intermittent FR_NOT_READY or mount failures can follow low-level init mismatch
Data mismatch only with DMA enabled suggests coherency alignment issue
debug_checks: Verify cache clean invalidate calls around each DMA transfer
Ensure sector buffers are aligned and sized to card block boundaries
Place DMA buffers in validated SRAM region with explicit MPU policy
Serialize FatFS operations during DMA transfer windows
Compare behavior with DMA disabled as a control test
possible_workarounds: Use non-cacheable DMA buffers with explicit alignment
Temporarily disable DMA template path to isolate root cause
Add conservative synchronization around file system access
constraints_or_limits: Performance trade-off is expected when disabling cache or DMA paths
Exact fix depends on memory map and MPU configuration
Requires end-to-end write then readback validation

diagnostic_cards.title: USB FS device not enumerating
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: Device is not detected by host or appears then disconnects during enumeration.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Full-speed internal PHY projects after firmware upgrade or CubeMX regeneration.
likely_causes: USB 48 MHz source is invalid or unstable
Descriptor tables have inconsistent lengths or class settings
Endpoint init sequence is incomplete
VBUS sensing and power mode configuration mismatch
Firmware version change introduced PCD behavior regression
confirmed_facts: FS enumeration depends on valid 48 MHz clock path
Descriptor integrity is mandatory for host acceptance
H7 USB behavior can differ across firmware versions
plausible_diagnosis: No host detection often indicates clock or pull-up condition issue
Detection then immediate failure points to descriptor endpoint mismatch
Version-specific regression suspected when old release works and new fails
debug_checks: Validate USB clock tree and exact 48 MHz generation
Run descriptor parser and compare against known-good device profile
Trace endpoint open sequence and class init callbacks
Check VBUS sensing and battery charging configuration
Compare behavior across firmware tags with same hardware
possible_workarounds: Pin to known-good firmware release during root-cause analysis
Use minimal CDC baseline project to isolate class-layer variables
Disable optional features and re-enable incrementally
constraints_or_limits: Host OS driver behavior can add external variability
Regression claims require side-by-side reproducible setup
Board-level power path issues can mimic stack bugs

diagnostic_cards.title: Ethernet throughput is too low on H7
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: Network is functional but throughput remains far below expected line-rate.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: STM32H7 Ethernet with lwIP under RTOS and high traffic concurrency.
likely_causes: Descriptor ring sizes are too small for traffic profile
Cache coherency around DMA descriptors and buffers is incomplete
pbuf allocation strategy causes fragmentation or copy overhead
Checksum offload settings are inconsistent between stack and driver
Legacy and new ETH driver assumptions are mixed
confirmed_facts: ETH descriptor handling and cache policy dominate throughput stability
Driver architecture changes can impact both performance and API expectations
Ring and buffer tuning is workload-dependent
plausible_diagnosis: Low throughput with occasional stalls indicates descriptor starvation
Throughput collapse under load suggests cache or semaphore path contention
CPU-heavy packet path indicates missing offload or excessive copies
debug_checks: Measure RX TX ring occupancy and drop counters
Audit cache maintenance around descriptors and payload buffers
Profile pbuf usage and copy count per packet
Verify checksum offload configuration consistency
Compare behavior with reworked ETH driver branch
possible_workarounds: Increase descriptor ring and pool sizes
Tune pbuf strategy for zero-copy where possible
Adopt validated driver branch with explicit migration checklist
constraints_or_limits: Optimization trade-offs depend on memory budget and latency targets
Driver migration can break compatibility with older code
Need controlled benchmarking before claiming gains

diagnostic_cards.title: I2C bus stuck low after error
diagnostic_cards.symptom_summary: After NACK timeout or noise event SDA stays low and bus transactions no longer progress.
diagnostic_cards.affected_context: Shared bus with multiple slaves or hot-plug prone environments under RTOS load.
likely_causes: Slave keeps SDA low due to incomplete transaction
Controller state machine remains in busy or error state
STOP condition is not generated after fault
Pull-up network is weak for bus capacitance
Error ISR path does not execute full recovery
confirmed_facts: Stuck-low is often a physical plus protocol recovery issue
Software recovery usually requires explicit clock toggling and peripheral reset
Filter and timing settings influence robustness against glitches
plausible_diagnosis: SDA low with SCL toggles implies slave-side lockup
Both lines low or floating indicates hardware pull-up or short issue
Frequent recurrence under noise suggests timing filter mismatch
debug_checks: Read bus line levels with scope before and after recovery attempt
Perform controlled SCL toggling and STOP generation sequence
Reset I2C peripheral and reinitialize timing and filters
Check pull-up resistance against bus capacitance
Log HAL error flags and state transitions
possible_workarounds: Implement bus recovery routine before full peripheral reset
Lower bus speed during unstable operation
Strengthen pull-ups or shorten bus segment for validation
constraints_or_limits: Recovery success depends on slave behavior and bus topology
Permanent hardware fault cannot be solved by software recovery
Requires electrical validation for durable resolution

likely_causes: Driver size bookkeeping overflows for large payloads
Data-width conversion path multiplies transfer size beyond expected field range
Local integration still uses affected HAL release
confirmed_facts: Issue reports indicate transfer-size handling risk on large CRYP DMA payloads
Interim mitigation should minimize blast radius and preserve rollback
Any local patch must be validated with representative vectors
plausible_diagnosis: Failure threshold around payload size boundaries indicates size-field limitation
Chunking large payloads avoids problematic boundary conditions
Patching without regression matrix can introduce cryptographic correctness risk
debug_checks: Reproduce failure with deterministic payload sizes around threshold
Verify encryption and decryption correctness with known vectors
Confirm DMA completion and status flags across chunk boundaries
Benchmark latency and CPU impact of workaround
Document exact HAL version and patch delta
possible_workarounds: Split payload into safe-size chunks with explicit context continuity
Apply minimal local patch limited to size handling path
Add runtime guard to reject unsupported transfer lengths
constraints_or_limits: Do not claim official fix until release notes or merged evidence confirms it
Local patch requires full validation matrix and rollback plan
Security-sensitive code path demands test-vector traceability
